title: Order Candidates by Ranked Ballots
statement:
Each candidate is an uppercase letter. Every ballot in ballots is a string that ranks all the candidates, best first, and all ballots rank the same set of candidates.

Order the candidates like this: the one with more first-place votes comes first. If two are tied on first places, compare their second-place votes, then third-place, and so on. If they are tied at every position, the one earlier in the alphabet comes first.

Return the final order as a string.

examples.why: Everyone has one first place. On second places C has 2, B has 1, A has 0. Looking only at first places, or falling back to the alphabet too early, gives "ABC".
M wins on first places. K and P tie on first (1 each), on second (1 each) and on third (2 each), so the alphabet decides: K before P.
One ballot decides everything. The alphabet is only a last resort.

constraints: All ballots have the same length and the same letters
Each ballot uses each letter once
hints: Summarise each candidate by how many votes they got at each position.
Build a table count[letter][position]. Comparing two candidates is then comparing their rows position by position.
Sort the letters with a comparator: the first position where the rows differ decides (more votes first); if none differ, compare the letters.

explain.intuition:
The rule compares candidates position by position, so precompute exactly that: for every candidate, a row of counts [firsts, seconds, thirds, …]. Comparing two candidates is now comparing two rows the way you compare words in a dictionary, except bigger counts win.

That makes it an ordinary sort with a custom comparator, the same thing you do when sorting table rows by several columns. The alphabetical rule is just the final column.
steps: Let k be the ballot length. Make count[letter], an array of k zeros, for each letter on the first ballot.
For every ballot and every position p, increase count[ballot[p]][p].
Sort the letters. For two letters, find the first position where their counts differ; the larger count goes first.
If all positions tie, the alphabetically smaller letter goes first. Join the sorted letters.
pitfalls: Ranking by total points (like k for first, k − 1 for second). That is a different voting rule and gives different results.
Sorting by first places only and then alphabetically, skipping the later positions.
Getting the comparator direction wrong: more votes must sort earlier, but the alphabet tie-break is ascending.

solutions.title: Recount inside the comparator
solutions.idea: Sort the letters; whenever two are compared, scan all ballots position by position to count their votes.

solutions.title: Count table plus custom sort
solutions.idea: Count votes per letter and position once, then sort the letters by their count rows, larger first, alphabet last.

followups: Ballots may rank only some candidates. How do you treat candidates a ballot leaves out?
Ballots arrive as a stream and you must show the current order after each one. What can you update incrementally?
